strengths: Unified multimodal formulation: Decoupling flow time dimensions ($t$ for discrete atom types via CTMC, $s$ for continuous coordinates and lattice parameters via Riemannian ODE) allows a single model to seamlessly perform crystal structure prediction (CSP), de novo generation (DNG), and structure-conditioned atom type generation (ATG) as different trajectories in $(t,s)$ space without task-specific architectures or retraining.

Effective soft inductive bias for Transformers: The proposed lexicographical atom ordering (combining electronegativity and Wyckoff site symmetry) paired with hierarchical inter- and intra-orbit permutation augmentation dramatically curtails the factorial permutation search space (by over 11 orders of magnitude for $N=20$) while preserving physical equivalences. This allows standard Diffusion Transformers (DiT) to preserve realistic space-group distributions without collapsing to low-symmetry groups (like $P1$) or requiring explicit structural template conditioning.

Comprehensive and rigorous empirical evaluation: The paper evaluates across two prominent benchmarks (MP-20 and the larger, chronologically split MPTS-52) and uses standardized evaluation protocols (LeMat-GenBench with an ensemble of three state-of-the-art MLIPs: MACE-MP, UMA, Orb-v3). MCFlow demonstrates strong performance, outperforming baselines in CSP RMSE and MPTS-52 match rates, as well as leading thermodynamic stability metrics in DNG.

Thorough ablations: The authors provide detailed ablation experiments validating the necessity of decoupled time axes over coupled noise schedules (Table H.8), confirming the benefits of unified training without catastrophic interference (Table H.7), and isolating the impact of atom ordering, hierarchical permutations, and noisy guidance.
weaknesses: Ambiguity in CSP inference ordering: The paper explains that training sorts atoms lexicographically first by electronegativity and second by Wyckoff letter. However, during CSP inference, only composition is known—Wyckoff positions are unknown a priori. While sorting by electronegativity groups atoms by element, the manuscript does not explicitly specify how atoms of the same element are ordered when initial fractional coordinates are sampled from the prior, or how sensitive test-time CSP performance is to intra-element token permutations at initialization.

Symmetry-dependence during data preprocessing: The training pipeline relies on space group and Wyckoff position extraction (e.g., via SpaceGroupAnalyzer with a tolerance threshold). Real-world experimental crystal structures frequently suffer from thermal noise, minor structural distortions, or partial occupancies, which can make space group assignment sensitive to tolerance parameters and limit applicability to disordered or uncurated datasets.

Novelty-stability trade-off at larger model scales: In the de novo generation experiments (Table 2), scaling from MCFlow-S to MCFlow-L increases thermodynamic stability (from 11.7% to 18.8%) but results in a steep decline in novelty (from 52.2% down to 18.6% with pre-relaxation), suggesting that larger models tend to memorize or heavily favor known training chemistry/structural motifs.

strengths: Elegantly unifies crystal structure prediction (CSP), de novo generation (DNG), and structure-conditioned atom type generation (ATG) into a single flow model by decoupling modality-specific time axes ($t$ for discrete atom types via CTMC, $s$ for continuous coordinates/cell parameters via ODE).

Addresses the lack of crystallographic and permutation inductive biases in Diffusion Transformers (DiT) via a principled composition- and symmetry-aware lexicographical ordering (electronegativity and Wyckoff positions) paired with hierarchical inter- and intra-orbit permutation augmentations, drastically reducing the effective permutation space without requiring rigid explicit structural templates.

Comprehensive and rigorous evaluation across multiple standardized benchmarks and modern protocols (e.g., LeMat-GenBench with an ensemble of MACE-MP, UMA, and Orb-v3; MPTS-52 for up to 52 atoms/cell; polymorph-aware METRe metric).

Strong empirical results across all supported tasks: competitive with or outperforming specialized baselines in CSP and DNG, notably excelling in thermodynamic stability and symmetry preservation while reducing low-symmetry mode collapse (Figure 4).
Detailed ablation studies that clearly isolate the benefits of decoupled time axes, electronegativity ordering, hierarchical permutations, and noisy guidance.
weaknesses: Test-time ordering ambiguity in CSP is somewhat undertreated: while the paper notes that Wyckoff positions are unknown at inference time for CSP, it does not explicitly clarify how atoms of the identical element type are ordered when feeding the conditioning composition into the DiT during inference, given that training sorts them by Wyckoff letter.

As model capacity scales from MCFlow-S to MCFlow-L, sample novelty drops considerably (e.g., in LeMat-GenBench pre-relaxation, novelty falls from 52.2% to 18.6%, leading to lower SUN/MSUN rates despite higher validity/stability), indicating a significant bias toward memorizing training distributions as model size increases.

The data preparation relies on robust determination of space groups and Wyckoff positions (e.g., via spglib / pymatgen SpaceGroupAnalyzer), making the training pipeline sensitive to symmetry-finding tolerances and restricting applicability to well-ordered crystalline systems (as noted in limitations).

strengths: Unified multimodal formulation for crystal generation: Formulating crystal structure prediction (CSP), de novo generation (DNG), and structure-conditioned atom type generation (ATG) as different trajectories in a 2D time plane $(t, s)$ is conceptually clean and avoids maintaining separate task-specific models.

Effective soft inductive bias for Transformers: By sorting atoms lexicographically via electronegativity and Wyckoff positions combined with hierarchical inter- and intra-orbit permutation augmentations, the DiT backbone captures crystallographic and compositional priors from data without needing explicit space group conditioning or rigid structural template modules.

Thorough empirical evaluation across multiple tasks: The method is comprehensively evaluated on established benchmarks (MP-20 and MPTS-52 for CSP; LeMat-GenBench for DNG; ATG and atom substitution). On MPTS-52 and on thermodynamic stability metrics (energy above hull, relaxation RMSD, stability rate), MCFlow achieves strong and competitive results.

Extensive analysis and ablation studies: The paper provides rich supplementary investigations, including polymorph-aware METRe evaluation, template-conditioned comparisons, computational efficiency analysis (Table H.1), noisy guidance sensitivity, and decoupled vs. coupled time trajectories.
weaknesses: Ambiguity in atom ordering during CSP inference: During training, atoms are lexicographically sorted first by Pauling electronegativity and second by Wyckoff position. However, in CSP, the model is conditioned only on chemical composition, so Wyckoff positions are unknown a priori. The manuscript does not sufficiently formalize how ties among identical elements are broken at inference time and how robust the DiT is to the resulting train-test ordering discrepancy.

Significant drop in novelty for de novo generation (DNG): In Table 2, while MCFlow achieves high stability, the novelty of generated crystals drops substantially as model capacity increases (Novelty: 52.2% for MCFlow-S, 25.4% for MCFlow-B, and only 18.6% for MCFlow-L, compared to 60-70% for MatterGen, WyFormer, and DiffCSP). This suggests that the larger models are heavily biased toward memorizing or reproducing known training structures.

Modest multi-sample CSP performance on MP-20: In Table 1, multi-sample (20) match rates on MP-20 show that MCFlow (77.8% for S, 77.1% for B, 76.1% for L) does not improve upon existing baselines such as CrystalFlow (78.34%) or DiffCSP (77.93%), with larger models exhibiting slightly lower match rates.

Lack of exact crystallographic symmetry guarantees: Because symmetry is incorporated purely as a soft inductive bias via ordering and data augmentation rather than exact geometric/space-group equivariance, generated structures can exhibit minor symmetry-breaking distortions that still require downstream relaxation tools to recover ideal crystallographic coordinates.

strengths: Unified framework: The proposed multimodal flow matching formulation cleanly decouples flow time axes for discrete atom types (CTMC) and continuous geometric variables (Riemannian ODE on the flat torus and Euclidean space), enabling any-to-any conditional generation (CSP, DNG, and atom type generation) within a single trained model without task-specific retraining.

Clever soft inductive bias for Transformers: By introducing lexicographical ordering (via electronegativity and Wyckoff site symmetry) paired with hierarchical inter- and intra-orbit permutation augmentations, the framework injects physical and crystallographic priors into a standard Diffusion Transformer (DiT) without needing rigid template conditioning or complex asymmetric unit (ASU) constraints.

Comprehensive empirical evaluation: The paper demonstrates strong results across two inorganic datasets (MP-20 and MPTS-52) across three distinct tasks. In particular, MCFlow shows substantial gains on MPTS-52, which features larger unit cells, and produces structures with superior thermodynamic stability and realistic space group distributions compared to unconstrained baselines.

Thorough ablations and sensitivity analysis: The paper includes rigorous ablations isolating the importance of inter- and intra-orbit permutations, positional embeddings, and noisy guidance hyperparameters, along with model scaling analyses.
weaknesses: Ambiguity in atom ordering during CSP inference: While training sorts atoms lexicographically by electronegativity and Wyckoff positions, during CSP inference the Wyckoff positions of the target crystal are unknown a priori. While elements can be sorted by electronegativity, the residual order among identical atoms within a composition cannot use true Wyckoff positions. The manuscript should explicitly detail how the input sequence of atoms is ordered during CSP inference and quantify any sensitivity to this arbitrary initial ordering.

Incremental multimodal flow formulation: Decoupling modality-specific time axes for any-to-any generation closely follows prior paradigms in multimodal generative modeling (such as MultiFlow and Rojas et al., 2025). The primary novelty lies in the application and symmetry-aware ordering/augmentation for crystalline lattices rather than the underlying flow machinery itself.

Computational scaling with sequence length: Although the model evaluates up to 52 atoms in MPTS-52, the all-atom transformer relies on standard self-attention scaling quadratically with the number of atoms. A discussion or empirical profiling of memory/runtime overhead for larger supercells (e.g., >100 atoms) would clarify practical scaling limits.

strengths: Unified multimodal formulation: Decoupling flow time variables into a 2D time plane (t for discrete atom types via CTMC, s for continuous crystal structures via ODE) enables a single trained DiT model to perform crystal structure prediction (CSP), de novo generation (DNG), and atom type generation (ATG) without task-specific retraining or structural template modules.

Effective soft inductive bias for symmetry: Lexicographical ordering by Pauling electronegativity and Wyckoff orbits, coupled with hierarchical inter- and intra-orbit permutation augmentations, effectively guides the transformer to capture crystallographic symmetry distributions (avoiding collapse to low-symmetry P1 modes as seen in Figure 4) without requiring rigid space-group constraints.

Comprehensive empirical evaluation: Evaluated across two standard benchmarks (MP-20 and the larger MPTS-52 dataset) across three distinct generation settings. Results show competitive or superior performance, particularly in single-sample CSP accuracy, structural stability metrics (lower relaxation steps and RMSE in Figure 5), and scalability to larger unit cells.

Solid ablations and methodology: The paper provides clear ablations isolating the impact of inter- and intra-orbit permutations, positional embeddings, and noisy guidance, as well as an analysis of permutation space reduction (Appendix D) and model scaling behavior (Appendix H.3).
weaknesses: Clarification needed on inference-time atom ordering for CSP: During training, atoms are lexicographically ordered first by Pauling electronegativity and then by Wyckoff letter. However, in crystal structure prediction (CSP), Wyckoff positions are unknown at inference time because only the chemical composition is provided. The paper notes this limitation of prior work in Section 3.2, but does not explicitly describe how the tie-breaking between identical elements is handled at inference time in Algorithm 2 when Wyckoff labels are unavailable.

Modest multi-sample CSP gains on MP-20: While MCFlow demonstrates superior single-sample CSP performance and faster trajectory saturation (Figure 3), its 20-sample match rate on MP-20 (77.12% for Base, 76.08% for Large) is slightly below task-specific baselines such as CrystalFlow (78.34%) and DiffCSP (77.93%).

Limited evaluation for atom type generation (ATG): The structure-conditioned atom type generation experiment in Table 3 only compares against a single deterministic baseline (CGCNN from 2018). Including more contemporary probabilistic/generative baselines or masked element prediction baselines would make this evaluation more convincing.

Incomplete DNG metrics on MPTS-52: For MPTS-52 de novo generation (Table 12), only structural and compositional validities are reported, omitting the full suite of stability, uniqueness, and novelty (S.U.N. / MS.U.N.) metrics reported for MP-20.

strengths: Unified Multi-Task Framework: MCFlow introduces a principled formulation decoupling flow time variables for discrete atom types (via CTMC) and continuous crystal structures (via Riemannian flow on the torus and Euclidean flow on lattice parameters). This enables crystal structure prediction (CSP), de novo generation (DNG), and atom type generation (ATG) within a single trained network without task-specific fine-tuning or separate architectures.

Effective Inductive Bias for Transformers: The paper addresses the lack of geometric and crystallographic symmetry in standard Diffusion Transformers (DiTs) via a lexicographical atom ordering (electronegativity and Wyckoff positions) paired with hierarchical inter- and intra-orbit permutation augmentations, effectively narrowing down the permutation search space by orders of magnitude.

Comprehensive Empirical Evaluation: Evaluated across standard MP-20 and the larger, chronologically split MPTS-52 benchmarks, MCFlow exhibits competitive performance against task-specialized baselines. In particular, it shows strong scaling behavior across parameter scales (34M to 464M) and better retention of true crystallographic space-group distributions without mode-collapsing to P1.

Thorough Ablations and Analysis: The submission provides detailed ablations investigating the role of inter/intra-orbit permutations, positional embeddings, integration step efficiency, and the application of noisy guidance.
weaknesses: Test-Time Ordering Ambiguity in CSP: Section 3.2 and Section 4.1 discuss ordering atoms by electronegativity and Wyckoff position during training. However, in standard CSP, only chemical composition (atom counts and types) is provided at inference time, meaning Wyckoff positions are unknown. The paper does not sufficiently clarify how atoms of the same element are ordered during CSP inference, nor does it quantify how sensitive DiT generation is to arbitrary initial permutations within identical elements at test time.

Overstated 'Any-to-Any' Scope: While framed broadly as 'any-to-any modality generation', the system effectively couples only two modalities (atom types and geometric structure). Other relevant crystal modalities—such as space group labels, chemical properties (band gap, formation energy), or partial coordinate scaffolding—are not integrated into the flow plane.

Post-Hoc Template Filtering in Appendix H.1: In Table 11, the comparison against template-conditioned methods computes metrics only on generated samples matching the target template. This post-hoc filtering requires clearer discussion, as discarding non-matching samples can inflate match rates compared to end-to-end conditional generation.

Trade-offs in DNG Metrics: While validity and metastability metrics are strong, Table 2 indicates that the strict Stability-Uniqueness-Novelty (S.U.N.) rate does not consistently improve over baselines (e.g., MCFlow-B reaches 3.3%, comparable to FlowMM at 3.3% and lower than SGFM at 4.7%), showing that high valid rates do not immediately translate to higher thermodynamic ground-state novelty.
